source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet: Test-Time Learning with Adaptive Memory
finding: Smaller models get weak or negative gains from a self-curated memory. The paper says memory needs a base model that makes correct solutions often enough to fill the memory with good strategies.
numbers: Table 3. Claude 3.5 Haiku accuracy BL / DC- / DC-Cu / DC-RS: AIME 2024 10.0/26.7/36.7/30.0; AIME 2025 0.0/13.3/13.3/10.0; GPQA-Diamond 43.4/41.9/43.7/49.0. GPT-4o-mini: AIME 2024 16.7/20.0/13.3/13.3; AIME 2025 10.0/13.3/13.3/16.7; GPQA-Diamond 34.3/34.3/33.8/32.3. AIME sets have 30 questions each, so one question is 3.3 points.
quote: smaller models, such as GPT-4o-mini, show limited gains under DC
limits: Tiny test sets (30 items). Memory was written by the same small model, so this does not test a strong model's library handed to a weak solver. R1 and o1 models showed minimal or inconsistent gains.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a merged library helps a weak solver. If the solver is weak, the merge step and the use step both fail. Gate library use on solver strength or test it first.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Sleep-time Compute: Beyond Inference Scaling at Test-time
finding: Pre-computing over a shared context pays off when several related questions follow, and more when the question is predictable from the context. The text gives the 2.5x cost figure but no explicit break-even question count.
numbers: Multi-Query GSM-Symbolic P1: 1095 contexts, 1095 original + 10,948 generated questions (about 10 per context). P2: 500 contexts, 500 + 4,997. Cost model weights a test-time token as 10 sleep-time tokens (t=10). Reported 2.5x lower average cost per query; about 5x less test-time compute at equal accuracy on Stateful GSM-Symbolic/AIME. Sleep-time compute generally Pareto-dominates pass@k at equal test-time tokens. Accuracy gap widens across five predictability bins.
quote: sleep-time compute is more effective in settings where the query is more easily predictable
limits: The t=10 weight is an assumption about latency pricing. Extra questions were written by o3-mini, so they are cleanly related to the context. Predictability is measured as question log-prob under the context, which needs the future question, so it cannot be used as a live trigger as is. No break-even count is stated in the text I read.
agent_relevance: Merge offline only when later related tasks are expected (about 10 per context here). With fewer, the offline cost may not be repaid at t=10. A count of related stored cases is a plausible proxy for predictability.

source: Dai et al. (2026) RecMem: Recurrence-based Memory Consolidation for Efficient and Effective Long-Running LLM Agents
finding: Run the expensive LLM consolidation only when similar interactions have recurred enough times. This cut construction tokens by about 87% and kept the best overall score among memory systems. A higher recurrence count hurt.
numbers: LoCoMo with GPT-4.1-mini: 193.2K construction tokens vs 1520.8K (Mem0) and 1459.9K (A-Mem), reductions 87.3% and 86.8%. Defaults: similarity 0.7 and count 5 (LoCoMo); 0.6 and 4 (LongMemEval-S). Overall score 81.1 at count 5 vs 78.9 at count 6. Token cost fell smoothly as count rose; accuracy did not.
limits: Conversation memory (facts, episodes), not rules or procedures. Thresholds were tuned per benchmark. No random-cluster control found. Single arXiv preprint.
agent_relevance: A count-and-similarity trigger is a tested, cheap alternative to a fixed merge schedule. Expect a sweet spot: too late means big clusters and lost detail.

source: Ye et al. (2026) Auto-Dreamer: Learning Offline Memory Consolidation for Language Agents
finding: Rewriting a region of the memory bank offline (new entries plus older entries the agent recently retrieved) shrinks the bank 6x to 11x. An untrained rewriter already gets most of the size cut and some of the accuracy gain. Too-frequent and too-rare consolidation both lose accuracy. Over-compression drops task details.
numbers: Table 2 success rate / bank tokens. ALFWorld: writer-only 48.0 / 50,735; untrained rewrite 59.2 / 6,900; trained 60.2 / 10,954. ScienceWorld: 29.6 / 61,679; 31.4 / 5,700; 41.1 / 6,947. WebArena: 44.2 / 6,421; 46.6 / 1,067; 52.3 / 927. Cadence sweep k in {1,5,20} vs main k=8 (ALFWorld) and k=10 (ScienceWorld): worse at k=1 and k=20 on ScienceWorld; ALFWorld within about 5 points, k=5 +1.1. Failure: look_at_obj_in_light family lost location details; excluding it widens the trained-vs-untrained margin from +1.0 to +4.9 (65.8 vs 60.9).
limits: Authors state no seed or task-order variance; several ALFWorld margins are small. Region is chosen by recency and retrieval, not by measured overlap, and there is no random-region control. Trained with RL on ScienceWorld.
agent_relevance: Supports a periodic (every ~5 to 10 tasks) merge that works on recent plus co-retrieved items. Keep task-specific details (exceptions) next to generic rules.

source: Grand et al. (2024) LILO: Learning Interpretable Libraries by Compressing and Documenting Code (Table 1 and text, ICLR)
finding: Giving an LLM solver a library of symbolic (Stitch) abstractions without names or docs did not help and often hurt. Adding LLM-written names and docstrings (AutoDoc) fixed most of it. A merged library is only useful if the solver can read it.
numbers: Online synthesis, solve rate. Text reports change from adding Stitch with no AutoDoc vs the plain LLM solver: -30.60 (REGEX), -2.91 (CLEVR), -11.11 (LOGO). Checking Table 1: the REGEX figure equals the difference of best-of-3 maxima (90.00 vs 59.40); mean-to-mean is -22.93 (76.13 vs 53.20). CLEVR and LOGO match mean differences. AutoDoc then adds +9.73 (REGEX) and +2.27 (CLEVR) over no AutoDoc, +0.00 on LOGO.
limits: Code-like DSL tasks, 3 seeds, high variance (REGEX std 12 to 14). The text mixes max and mean deltas. Shows early or unreadable merging can hurt, but not how long until it pays.
agent_relevance: A merged rule must be named and explained in the solver's own language. A rule written as a bare compressed pattern can lower accuracy below no library.

source: Grand et al. (2024) LILO appendix: LLM Compressor vs Stitch on frozen program sets
finding: Closest head-to-head of overlap finders on code. Symbolic Stitch finds shared structure; GPT-4 asked to find abstractions does not. Both random and clustered example sampling were tried for GPT-4.
numbers: Same frozen set of solved programs given to both. Stitch compression ratio 1.5x to 3.5x, rising as more programs were solved. GPT-4 compressor about 1.0x (no compression). Only 19.01% (998 of 5250) of GPT-4 abstractions were valid expressions. GPT-4 abstractions were shorter and lower arity. Authors dropped the LLM compressor from further runs.
limits: Three DSLs only, GPT-4 of 2023, one prompt format. Separate clustered-versus-random compression numbers were in a figure I could not read from text. No test on free-text rules, no entity-overlap or embedding-only finder.
agent_relevance: For structured code-like rules, use a symbolic or programmatic overlap finder and let the LLM do naming and use. Do not ask the LLM to find the shared part by itself on structured rules.

source: Grand et al. (2024) LILO appendix A.3: random vs cosine-similarity example selection for the solver prompt
finding: Choosing prompt examples by similarity did not reliably beat random choice in LILO. The authors saw similarity fooled by shared surface words.
numbers: Final solve rate mean, random vs similarity: REGEX 77.07 vs 71.33; CLEVR 96.76 vs 97.41; LOGO 48.95 vs 53.15. Authors chose random sampling for main results, citing no evidence for added complexity.
limits: This is example selection, not rule merging. Three seeds, large variance. Table text is partly garbled in extraction, so the row assignment was checked against the prose.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence that overlap-based grouping beats random at the retrieval step. Shared surface words give false overlap; use structure, not words.

source: Gao et al. (2024) ReGAL: Refactoring Programs to Discover Generalizable Abstractions (ablation Table 3)
finding: ReGAL groups examples by embedding of the query (Ward clustering), orders groups short-to-long, and refactors each group. Removing the easy-to-hard order hurts in all three domains. The paper has no ablation of clustering versus random grouping that I could find.
numbers: Dev splits, CodeLlama-13B. Full REGAL vs no curriculum (random cluster order): LOGO 55.0 vs 36.3 (-18.7); Date 77.0 vs 56.6 (-20.4); TextCraft 34.12 vs 28.78. Other removals: no retry LOGO 48.3, Date 51.9; no pruneCodeBank Date 65.5, TextCraft 25.26; no editCodeBank Date 69.6.
limits: Ordering evidence holds in three code-like domains, one model. 'Order' here is easy to hard across clusters, not within-family-first-then-across. Grouping by overlap was never compared with random groups.
agent_relevance: Order merges easy to hard. Prune and edit steps matter. The core question (does overlap grouping beat random grouping) is still untested here.

source: Berlot-Attwell, Rudzicz and Si (2024) Library Learning Doesn't: The Curious Case of the Single-Use 'Library'
finding: Two published math library learners (LEGO-Prover, TroVE) hardly reuse what they learn. Removing the ability to reuse leaves accuracy the same or higher. Gains come from self-correction and majority vote.
numbers: LEGO-Prover logs: 127, 135, 111, 122 problems solved per split; at most 1 or 2 lemmas reused verbatim, none reused twice. TroVE on MATH test: 15 learned functions, learned for 3 of 7 subjects; 3 correct reuses in 3,201 test questions. No-reuse ablation vs reproduced TroVE: counting 0.250 vs 0.236, geometry 0.050 vs 0.058, intermediate algebra 0.134 vs 0.120, number theory 0.290 vs 0.258 (5 trials).
limits: CodeLlama-7B for TroVE; small differences. Answers gap 3 in the negative for these two systems: on math, a library did not pay for itself once sampling was matched.
agent_relevance: On free-text math, do not count a gain unless it beats the same agent with majority vote and the same tokens. Measure reuse rate directly.

source: Berlot-Attwell, Rudzicz and Si (2025) LLM Library Learning Fails: A LEGO-Prover Case Study
finding: With compute matched, a plain Draft-Sketch-Prove baseline matches or beats LEGO-Prover. Reported gains vanish once cost is counted.
numbers: Fixed attempts, miniF2F test (DSP vs LEGO-Prover): gpt-4o-mini 35.9% vs 25.8% (100 attempts); gpt-4o 23.1 vs 29.3; o3-mini 19.4 vs 27.8 (subsets of 20% or 5%). Per-attempt cost ratio LEGO-Prover to DSP: 5.84, 5.94, 14.23 (o3-mini). At matched GPU budget DSP is within one standard deviation or better (authors, Table 5).
limits: Cost is estimated from API price as a proxy. One system. The matched-cost table is garbled in the text extraction, so only the prose claim and the cost ratios are used.
agent_relevance: Token-matched testing is the required standard. Treat any claim of library gains without it as unproven.

source: Moll et al. (2026) GRASP: Gated Regression-Aware Skill Proposer for Self-Improving LLM Agents
finding: A held-out probe of previously failing and previously passing episodes, with a hard regression budget, is what makes skill edits safe. Writing skills with no gate is no better than no skills.
numbers: MedAgentBench, gpt-oss-120b: no skills 40.6; GRASP 88.8. Ablations: no failure grouping 84.4; no regression budget 81.8; fixes-only and append-only 80.2; no gate at K=1 40.1 (matches no-skills 40.6); no gate at K=4 63.5. Matched-compute control (run the probe, then pick an edit without its score) 70.8 and 67.2 (random pick). Granting the same gate to five baselines lifts in-domain by +1.6 to +15.0 at K=1, but out-of-domain change is about -0.1 (Table 5). Probe: 36 episodes, 411 probe calls per batch.
limits: Clinical FHIR agent tasks, rules are behavioral instructions, not merged rules. Probe is a check on stored cases, so cost grows with probe size. Authors say probe size trades against gate reliability. Not a measured count of bad rules admitted.
agent_relevance: Best measured guard against a merge that breaks an old case: re-run the stored pass and fail cases and cap allowed regressions. The gate matters more than the writing.

source: Moll et al. (2026) GRASP, cross-model and cross-benchmark transfer (Tables 2 and 3)
finding: A stronger writer's gated library improves weaker executors. A weaker writer's library applied to a stronger executor does worse than self-written. The asymmetry did not appear for the baselines. Libraries moved to a hard new benchmark can degrade.
numbers: Libraries written by GPT-5.4 (low) improve every executor on out-of-domain task types. On FHIR-AgentBench, self-training lifts gpt-oss-120b from 51.5% to 58.2% (+6.8, 95% CI 3.7 to 10.0), while every library transferred in lowered it (MedAgentBench 47.2, v2 45.7, DBBench 48.3). MedAgentBench skills on v2: 78.1 test, 86.7 OOD vs v2 self-training 76.9, 86.0.
limits: Five models, clinical tasks. The cross-model table cells were not fully legible in the text extraction; findings are from the prose. Same source as d11.
agent_relevance: Strong-to-weak transfer can work when the library is gated and bounded. Reverse direction and new domains need a gate again.

source: Huang et al. (2026) From Raw Experience to Skill Consumption: A Systematic Study of Model-Generated Agent Skills
finding: Model-written skills help on average but a quarter of extractor-target pairs get worse. Skill value does not follow model size. An LLM judge reading two skills picks the better one no better than chance.
numbers: Across five domains: positive transfer in 75% of extractor-target entries, negative in 25%. Negative rate 13% on SpreadsheetBench and SWE-bench-Verified, 47% on ALFWorld. Lightweight Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite was the best extractor on SpreadsheetBench; GPT-5.4 ranked last there despite the best baseline. Unguided pairwise judge accuracy 46.4%; on pairs with the largest utility gap (5 points or more) it picked the better skill only 15.8% of the time; rubric-guided judge 73.8%. Each evaluation run three times.
limits: Skills are extracted procedures, not merged rules. The rubric was derived from the same data, so 73.8% may be optimistic.
agent_relevance: Review by an LLM reader is a weak guard: a rule that reads well often performs worse. Use measured outcomes on stored cases instead.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: An Empirical Study of Experience-Following Behavior
finding: Agents copy the output of the most similar stored record, so bad records spread. Adding everything lowers accuracy below a fixed small memory. Selective addition and history-based deletion help.
numbers: Success or accuracy, fixed memory vs add-all vs strict (oracle) selection: RegAgent 67.53 / 55.48 / 70.95; EHRAgent 16.75 / 13.05 / 38.50; AgentDriver 40.11 / 32.32 / 51.00; CIC-IoT 71.50 / 59.90 / 85.40. Fine-tuned coarse judge (C3) 67.35 / 34.66 / 47.37 / 79.50. History-based deletion with strict evaluator: EHRAgent 38.67 to 42.06 (memory 1012 to 784), CIC-IoT 85.40 to 89.60; RegAgent 70.95 to 69.80. With the coarse evaluator it helped EHRAgent (25.91 to 33.55) and hurt AgentDriver (36.92 to 34.00). Retained vs deleted correctness: CIC-IoT 78.9% vs 56.7% (GPT-4o-mini judge).
limits: Stores raw records, not merged rules. Main model GPT-4o-mini. Read through a page converter, so numbers were not cross-checked against the PDF tables.
agent_relevance: Add-all is harmful. Gate additions and delete low-utility items by later outcomes. A merged rule is a record that will be copied, so its errors replicate.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners (main results and ablations)
finding: Rules (insights) and raw cases (retrieved trajectories) win on different tasks, and the two together win overall. The routing signal in the paper is the task type, judged by the authors, not learned. Random example choice hurt, and similarity-based choice was best.
numbers: Insights-only vs retrieve-only success: HotpotQA 36% vs 31%; ALFWorld 50% vs 55%; WebShop 37% vs 38% (scores 0.675 vs 0.67). Authors: gpt-4 insight extractor beats gpt-3.5-turbo; learned insights beat hand-crafted; adding reflections to insight extraction hurt. Random sampling of in-context trajectories on ALFWorld gave a significant drop vs task-similarity retrieval (ExpeL 59.0; the other table cells are garbled in extraction).
limits: Three environments, four-fold validation. No automatic router tested. Paper explains the split by reasoning-heavy vs action-specific tasks.
agent_relevance: Keep rules and raw cases as two stores. Route by whether the task needs general guidance (rules) or exact action sequences (cases). Retrieve cases by task similarity, not at random.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory (online learning curve and cross-template results)
finding: AWM builds workflows from past examples and then builds larger workflows from earlier ones. Gains appear within tens of examples. Workflow memory is weaker when the new task does not match a past template.
numbers: Text: success rates 'gradually stabilize to the highest point in the early learning phase', improvement 'with merely tens of examples'; a figure annotation reads 'gap widens to 22.5 after 40 examples'. In the ReasoningBank paper, AWM fails to give gains and even degrades on the WebArena Multi (cross-website) subset.
limits: I could not read the underlying learning-curve numbers from text; figure annotation only. Offline AWM is weaker than online as the domain gap grows (paper text). WebArena and Mind2Web only.
agent_relevance: A task-count equivalent of 'time to gist' here is tens of tasks in web agents, not a year. Early workflows are simple and later ones compose them.

source: Ouyang et al. (2025) ReasoningBank: Scaling Agent Self-Evolving with Reasoning Memory (retrieval-count ablation)
finding: More retrieved memory items did not help. One retrieved experience helped most. Relevance and quality beat quantity.
numbers: WebArena success rate: no memory 39.0; 1 retrieved experience 49.7; 2 gives 46.5; 3 gives 45.5; 4 gives 44.4. Authors: excessive experiences may introduce conflicts or noise.
limits: This is the number retrieved per task, not library size or task count. Figure text was garbled; numbers are from the prose of Appendix C.1. Single benchmark.
agent_relevance: Cap how many merged rules enter a prompt. One well-matched rule can beat several.

source: Nagel, Sander, Diekelmann and Feld (2026) Sleep links gist abstraction to veridical memory. J Exp Psychol Learn Mem Cogn
finding: Peer-reviewed, preregistered, large online replication of Diekelmann et al. (2010) with the DRM false-memory task. Sleep had no main effect on false memories or on general memory. Gist appeared only in a conditional effect.
numbers: N = 104 sleep, 101 wake, 99 AM control, 94 PM control (398). No effect of sleep on false memories or general memory. Did not replicate 'sleep raises false memories when overall memory is low'. False memories rose after sleep when intrusion-adjusted memory was high.
limits: Abstract read only (PubMed); full text not opened. It is a DRM word-list test, not Durrant's statistical-learning task or Matorina's REM result, so it does not close that part of the gap. The gist reading is a post-hoc interpretation of an interaction.
agent_relevance: The sleep-gist story is weaker than textbook accounts. Use it as design inspiration, not as proof that offline merging works.

source: Cao et al. (2025) Analyzing Memory Effects in Large Language Models through the Lens of Cognitive Psychology
finding: LLMs show a small DRM-style false-memory effect: they say old to a never-shown lure word more than to unrelated words. Small local models showed essentially none.
numbers: Hit rate for studied words 1.000. Non-studied false alarm 0.053. Critical lure proportion old 0.114 (about double). Offline models (Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, Llama-3-8B) mostly recognized lures as new.
limits: Word-list recognition, not rule merging. Model names not tied to the 0.114 in the text I read. An analogue of confident unsupported generation from merged rules is not tested.
agent_relevance: Lure-like errors exist but are small. No direct LLM test of a merged rule causing unsupported output was found; the guard in d11 still applies.

source: Search-result summaries only: MOOM (2025) on merge strategies
finding: Search snippets say LLM-based merging beat embedding-based and rule-based merging under a memory cap. I did not open the paper.
numbers: Snippet: with a 50-item cap, MemScore rose from 1.189 (rule-based only) to 1.405 (LLM-based merging).
limits: Snippet only. Role-play dialogue memory. No random-merge control mentioned.
agent_relevance: Lead only. Do not cite without opening.

source: Search-result summaries only: strong-to-weak skill transfer (SKILL-DISCO 2026, ASDA 2026, Skill Transfer NeurIPS 2026)
finding: Snippets disagree. SKILL-DISCO reports a GPT-4o library helping small Qwen models most. ASDA reports skills from a weaker model hurting a stronger one. A NeurIPS paper says weak models get little value from strong-model skills unless the skill is adapted. I did not open these papers.
numbers: SKILL-DISCO snippet: Qwen3.5-9B with the GPT-4o library 98.5% on ALFWorld vs 96.3% for the inducer. ASDA snippet: -2.33 net.
limits: Snippets only; different benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Shows the question is open: GRASP (d12) and Huang (d13) are the opened evidence.
